records.source: Apache Kafka, Design: Message Delivery Semantics and Using Transactions
records.version_or_commit: docs/design/design.md on trunk at commit cd5ce522408d03c05726d71084ff4e632f378dbd, committed 2026-06-19; the site lists 4.3 as the current release line
records.finding: The three delivery semantics are properties of two separate problems, publishing and consuming, and the pairing is what decides them. A consumer that saves its position before processing gets at-most-once, and one that saves it after gets at-least-once, so the ordering of two lines of code is the guarantee. Exactly-once is available only where the position and the output can be committed together: inside Kafka the offset is written into the same transaction as the output topic, and outside it either the sink takes part in a two-phase commit or the consumer stores its offset in the same place as its output. The default without that arrangement is at-least-once, and the documentation says in its own voice that exactly-once claims elsewhere need their fine print read, because they usually assume nobody fails.
records.applicability_limits: Written about one broker's protocol. The transactional path needs a single consumer per partition in a group and a producer driving the offset commit, which is a specific runtime shape rather than a general recipe. Nothing here makes an arbitrary database, object store or HTTP endpoint transactional, and the offset-with-output trick needs a sink that can write both atomically, which many cannot.
records.counter_evidence: The same project's ecosystem markets exactly-once as a product feature while this page scopes it to read-process-write within Kafka. The correctness of the transaction protocol under fault has not been established by an independent analysis, and the Debezium maintainers record open issues against it (FRAG-DATA-ENGINEERING-06).
records.licence_evidence: The apache/kafka repository, which is where these documentation sources live, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.source: Apache Flink documentation, Timely Stream Processing
records.finding: There are two clocks and they are not interchangeable. Event time belongs to the record and never changes; processing time is whatever the machine's clock said when the record arrived, so it changes on every replay. A pipeline keyed on processing time gives a different answer each time it runs, which makes reprocessing meaningless. Progress in event time is carried by a watermark, a marker asserting that nothing older is still to come, and an operator with several inputs advances on the slowest of them. The documentation states plainly that no time can be named by which every record of a given timestamp will have arrived, so anything after the watermark is a late element and needs a declared destination.
records.applicability_limits: Describes one stream processor's implementation, and the watermark generator, allowed lateness and side output mechanics are Flink APIs rather than portable concepts. A venture running a nightly batch job has the same event-time and processing-time distinction but none of this machinery, so the idea transfers and the code does not.
records.counter_evidence: The mechanism is documented, not measured: no figure here says how much late data a real source produces or what a given lateness allowance recovers. Choosing the horizon is left entirely to the reader.
records.licence_evidence: The apache/flink repository, from which this documentation is generated, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.finding: The engine's exactly-once setting is a statement about its own state and its own stream positions, not about what the outside world sees. Restoring a consistent snapshot gives the job the state a failure-free run would have had, and that stops at the sink: carrying the property through to an external system needs the sink to take part, either by holding output in a transaction that commits with the checkpoint or by writing in a way that a repeat cannot change. The at-least-once setting exists as a deliberate trade for latency, which is the honest framing of the choice.
records.applicability_limits: The two-phase commit sink is only as good as the external system's transaction support and its tolerance of long-lived open transactions. Nothing here helps a sink that is a REST endpoint or a file drop. The latency argument for at-least-once is stated at a scale, a few milliseconds, that no scheduled venture pipeline operates at.
records.counter_evidence: The guarantee is asserted from the design, not demonstrated under adversarial failure, and the documentation gives no evidence that the transactional sinks recover correctly from every partial-commit state.
records.licence_evidence: The apache/flink repository, from which this documentation is generated, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.source: Akidau, Bradshaw, Chambers, Chernyak, Fernandez-Moctezuma, Lax, McVeety, Mills, Perry, Schmidt and Whittle, The Dataflow Model
records.study_design: Model and system description, validated against production use cases at Google rather than by controlled experiment
records.population: Unbounded, out-of-order datasets at global scale, including billing pipelines and video usage statistics
records.version_or_commit: Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, Volume 8, Number 12, pages 1792 onward, 2015
records.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 Unported, printed on the paper; paraphrase only, no wording reused
records.finding: Correctness, latency and cost cannot all be optimised at once over unbounded input, so a pipeline has to choose its point between them and say which it chose. The paper's central move is to stop treating an input as something that eventually becomes complete: new records arrive and old ones are retracted, and completeness is never known. It gives two named failure directions for the watermark, and both matter. Too fast, and records arrive behind it, so any pipeline that trusts it alone is knowingly lossy. Too slow, and one straggling record holds back the whole pipeline's output, so a global progress marker is also a latency risk. The conclusion is that a completeness signal alone is not enough, and a pipeline needs a separate answer for when it emits and what it does when more arrives afterwards.
records.applicability_limits: Written from Google-scale streaming, where the machinery it argues for exists. It says nothing about the cost of a batch pipeline that reruns a bounded window nightly, which is the shape most ventures actually run, and its examples assume a system with retraction and refinement semantics built in.
records.counter_evidence: The paper argues against running batch and streaming systems side by side on complexity grounds while its authors sell the unified alternative, so the comparison is not disinterested. It is also from 2015: several systems it dismisses on windowing or correctness grounds have changed substantially since, and its criticism of them should not be read forward.
records.licence_evidence: The licence notice printed in the first column of the paper's first page names the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0 Unported License.

records.source: Debezium documentation, Features, and the PostgreSQL connector's behaviour when things go wrong
records.version_or_commit: documentation on main; connectors/postgresql.adoc at commit d8e0de6ee63ddf66c7ea626d7f3a75894cba728e, 2026-08-14; latest release tag v3.6.1.Final
records.finding: Reading the database's own replication log rather than polling it changes what can be captured, not just how fast. Polling a modified-at column cannot see a delete, cannot see a row that changed twice between polls, and needs a column the data model did not otherwise want; the log sees every change in order, carries the previous values, and needs no schema change. The cost is a recorded position that has to survive restarts, and an initial snapshot for history the log no longer holds. The connector's own fault section is the part worth carrying: after an ungraceful stop it resumes from the last flushed position, so consumers should expect a replay of whatever came after it, and the change events are shaped to be idempotent so that replaying a sequence lands the same state. The log position travels in the event so a consumer can recognise a repeat.
records.applicability_limits: Needs a source database whose log the venture is allowed to read, which rules out most managed vendor systems and every third-party SaaS. The snapshot mechanism assumes the source will tolerate a long read, and the whole approach assumes an operator willing to run and monitor a connector process rather than a cron job.
records.counter_evidence: The advantage list is the project's own case for its own product. The strongest counter is that a source with no replication log access forces polling anyway, at which point the deletes the page criticises polling for missing have to be handled some other way, usually a soft-delete column the source owner has to agree to.
records.licence_evidence: The debezium/debezium repository, which holds this documentation source, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.version_or_commit: documentation/modules/ROOT/pages/configuration/eos.adoc at commit ced32f1b3b99, 2025-07-19; requires a connect runtime at 3.3.0 or later
records.finding: A maintainer stating the limits of its own strongest feature. The project provides at-least-once and has no deduplication layer of its own; exactly-once is available only by borrowing the connect framework's support, which rests on the broker's transactions. The page then says the project cannot tell whether that implementation is correct in every case, that no thorough analysis of it exists, that independent testing of other systems speaking the same protocol raised correctness concerns, and that several protocol issues are open. It carries a warning saying so. Six connectors can take part, the runtime must be distributed, and two settings must be right.
records.applicability_limits: Only meaningful where the pipeline already runs on that connect framework in distributed mode. A venture reading change events through an embedded engine, a server binary or any other transport gets at-least-once with no option, which is the ordinary case.
records.counter_evidence: This is itself the counter-evidence to the vendor consensus around exactly-once, and it cuts both ways: the page is one project's reading of another project's open issues rather than a finding about correctness, and open issues are not proof of a defect in practice.
records.licence_evidence: The debezium/debezium repository, which holds this documentation source, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.version_or_commit: format/spec.md at commit d8170b0dfae4, 2026-08-01; format versions 1, 2 and 3 adopted, version 4 under development and not adopted
records.finding: The primitive a reprocess needs is an atomic swap. Table state lives in a metadata file, every change writes a new one, and a commit is the pointer swap from the old to the new, which is what gives a reader a stable snapshot and a writer an all-or-nothing publish. Writers commit optimistically and retry against the new current version when someone else got there first, and the conditions a writer chooses to check are what set its isolation. Files are tracked individually rather than by directory, so a partition can be replaced without a rename or a directory shuffle. Row-level deletes come in two shapes with different costs: by file and row position, or by column value, and a delete file applies to older data files in the same partition.
records.applicability_limits: A format specification, not an engine: nothing here runs a merge, compacts a small-file mess or decides an isolation level for you, and the guarantees only hold if the engine implements the version it claims. Format version 3 features are not readable by every engine in the ecosystem, and a table written at a version the reader does not support is a broken pipeline rather than a slow one.
records.counter_evidence: A competing format with an equally active maintainer set and a different transaction log design covers the same ground (FRAG-DATA-ENGINEERING-12), so committing to this one is a bet in an unsettled format argument. The spec's own note that version 4 is unadopted is a reminder that the format is still moving.
records.licence_evidence: The apache/iceberg repository, which holds the specification source, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.source: Apache Iceberg documentation, Partitioning and Evolution
records.version_or_commit: docs site latest, 1.11.0; docs/docs/partitioning.md at commit 6a0d4a0f37a2, 2025-10-27
records.finding: The best statement anywhere of why a hand-maintained partition column is dangerous. When the writer supplies the partition value, nothing can check it: the wrong format, the wrong time zone, or the wrong source column, and the page names using the processing time instead of the event time as exactly that mistake, all produce answers that are quietly wrong rather than queries that fail. Readers inherit the same trap, because a query filtering only the real column scans everything, and the partition scheme cannot then be changed without breaking the queries that learned it. The alternative is to declare the partition as a transform of a real column and let the engine derive and apply it, which makes the value correct by construction and keeps queries independent of the physical layout. Evolving the layout is then a metadata change: existing files keep the old scheme, new files take the new one, both are planned separately, and nothing is rewritten.
records.applicability_limits: Hidden partitioning is a property of this format and its engines. A venture on plain directories of Parquet, or on a warehouse whose partitioning is a declared column, does not get it and has to defend the partition value some other way, usually by deriving it in one place in code and never by hand. The evolution story means a long-lived table can end up carrying several layouts at once, which is cheaper to declare than to reason about.
records.counter_evidence: The Hive comparison is the project arguing against the system it replaced, so it is not neutral. Partition evolution is presented as free because it moves no data, but the split planning it leaves behind is a real read-side cost the page does not quantify.
records.licence_evidence: The apache/iceberg repository, which holds the documentation source, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.version_or_commit: stable docs for 3.3.1; airflow-core/docs/best-practices.rst at commit 297b0c7abc16, 2026-08-14
records.finding: Three rules that together make a rerun mean something. A task is a transaction: it must not leave a half-written result behind, so a retry that inserts is a duplicate waiting to happen and an upsert is not. A task reads and writes a named window rather than whatever the source happens to hold at that moment, because the input can change between runs and then the same code produces two different answers with no way to tell which is right. And the window's boundaries come from the scheduler's data interval, never from the machine's clock: the documentation puts the current-time call out of bounds inside a task, and most firmly out of bounds in the arithmetic that matters, because it makes every run different.
records.applicability_limits: Written for one orchestrator and its scheduling model, and that model has changed across major versions, so the field names do not transfer. The rules themselves do. Nothing here addresses a pipeline with no orchestrator at all, where the window has to come from somewhere else, usually a high-water mark stored beside the output.
records.counter_evidence: This is asserted practice from a maintainer, with no measurement behind it: no study here compares reruns of window-parameterised pipelines against wall-clock ones. The advice is also, in part, a workaround for the scheduler's own design, which is why it reads as strongly as it does.
records.licence_evidence: The apache/airflow repository, which holds the documentation source, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.version_or_commit: current docs, requiring dbt Core 1.9 or later
records.licence: Apache-2.0 for the documentation repository; the rendered site's own terms were not read
records.finding: A worked shape for idempotent reprocessing that a small venture can actually run. The model declares which column carries the time an event happened, how wide a batch is, how far back to reprocess on an ordinary run, and the date history begins. Each batch is then an independent unit replaced atomically by whatever mechanism the warehouse offers, so a batch can be rerun over a period that already holds rows and the table it leaves behind does not change, and a failed run can be retried batch by batch rather than as a whole. Backfill is not a separate program: it is the same model run with an explicit start and end, so the code that repairs history is the code that produced it. Late arrivals get a declared lookback rather than a special path.
records.applicability_limits: Only the transformation half. It assumes the raw records already landed somewhere queryable and says nothing about how they got there. Every parent model has to declare its event-time column or the framework cannot narrow the read, and the batches scan everything. Support varies by warehouse, and the atomic replacement is whichever mechanism the adapter happens to have, so the guarantee is really the warehouse's.
records.counter_evidence: The lookback default reprocesses a single prior batch, which is a guess dressed as a default: nothing here says what lookback a given source needs, and a source with a longer tail loses records silently. The independence claim is per batch and does not survive a model whose output depends on rows outside its own window.
records.licence_evidence: The dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com repository, from which this page is published, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.licence: Apache-2.0 for the documentation repository; the rendered site's own terms were not read
records.finding: The reprocessing options laid out side by side with their costs, which is the fork most pipelines get wrong by never noticing it exists. Append adds rows and checks nothing, so a rerun duplicates. Delete then insert removes the rows matching a declared key and writes them again, which works where the key is not truly unique or where the warehouse has no merge. Merge updates what matches the key and inserts what does not, which is the safest and the most expensive, because deciding what matches means reading the destination. Replacing whole partitions is the cheapest way to correct a period, and it needs the table partitioned on the thing being corrected. Every one of them except append rests on a key, and the documentation is explicit that the value of the strategy is the reliability of that key; a merge with no key degrades into an append without saying so.
records.applicability_limits: Warehouse support is uneven and the table of what works where is part of the finding, not a footnote. The framing is transformation inside a warehouse and does not cover a pipeline landing files in object storage or writing to an operational database.
records.counter_evidence: No measurement is offered for any of the cost claims, and the advice to pick by data volume and key reliability leaves the actual threshold unstated. Nothing here compares the correctness of partition replacement against merge when the correction moves a row from one partition to another, which is the case where the two genuinely disagree.
records.licence_evidence: The dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com repository, from which this page is published, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.

records.source: Delta Lake documentation, Idempotent table writes in foreachBatch
records.version_or_commit: docs.delta.io latest; the feature is documented as available from Delta Lake 2.0.0; current release tag v4.3.1
records.licence: Apache-2.0 for the project; the documentation site's own terms were not read
records.finding: Idempotence can be a property of the write rather than of the data. A write carries an application identifier and a version number that only ever increases, the table records the highest version it has seen for that application, and a write whose version it has already seen is ignored. That makes a retry safe without a unique key in the rows and without reading the destination to compare, which is the cheap path when the payload has no natural key. The limitation is where the honesty is: the identifier and the counter are the whole mechanism, so restarting a job from a fresh checkpoint while keeping the old identifier makes the table reject the new writes, silently, because the counter began again below the recorded high-water mark.
records.applicability_limits: Tied to one table format and its streaming integration. The guarantee covers a repeat of the same logical write, not two different attempts to produce the same period, so it does not replace a partition-replacement or merge strategy for corrections. Nothing in it helps a downstream reader that already consumed a duplicate.
records.counter_evidence: The failure mode the page warns about, a stale identifier silently swallowing good writes, is the mirror of the problem the feature solves, and it fails quietly in the more dangerous direction. It is also a single-vendor mechanism with no equivalent in the competing format's specification, so it does not transfer.
records.licence_evidence: The delta-io/delta repository, which is the project this documentation covers, carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE file.
